short: Running computers that compete to add the next batch of transactions to a shared digital ledger such as Bitcoin's, earning new coins and fees.
kid: Lots of children race to solve a very hard puzzle. The first one to finish gets to write the next page in the class notebook and wins a few new stickers.
detail: Crypto mining is how proof-of-work blockchains such as Bitcoin record transactions and create new coins. Miners bundle waiting transactions into a block, then make quintillions of guesses per second, called hashes, looking for one that meets a target set by the network. The first to succeed adds the block and earns the block subsidy, newly created bitcoin, plus the fees users paid. The network resets the difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks, so a block arrives about every 10 minutes however many machines join. Mining is a business of cheap electricity and efficient specialised chips, and listed miners' shares swing with the bitcoin price; several have added AI data-centre businesses. The confusion to avoid: Ethereum stopped mining in September 2022, when it switched to proof of stake, where validators lock up coins instead of burning electricity.
example: Say a miner runs 1,000 machines, each drawing 3.5 kilowatts around the clock: 1,000 × 3.5 × 24 = 84,000 kWh a day, costing $4,200 at $0.05 per kWh. If the machines earn 0.06 BTC a day and bitcoin is at an assumed $80,000, revenue is $4,800, a daily margin of $600. After a halving the same machines would earn roughly half, about $2,400, less than the power bill, unless the price rises.
formula: Mining profit = (Coins earned × Coin price) − (Electricity used × Power price) − Other costs

short: The total computing power that miners devote to a blockchain such as Bitcoin, measured in guesses, or hashes, per second.
kid: Imagine many children all trying to guess a secret number at the same time. The more children guessing, and the faster they guess, the harder it is for one sneaky child to win every time.
detail: Hash rate measures how many hashes, or attempts at the mining puzzle, all miners on a proof-of-work network make each second. Bitcoin's is quoted in exahashes per second (EH/s), where one exahash is a billion billion hashes. Nobody counts it directly: it is estimated from how quickly blocks arrive at the current difficulty, so daily figures are noisy and analysts prefer seven-day averages. A higher hash rate makes the network costlier to attack, because an attacker would need to match most of it. It also signals miners' confidence, since they keep buying machines and paying power bills only if they expect to earn more than they spend. Hash rate often dips after a halving squeezes revenue. The confusion to avoid: more hash rate does not mean faster transactions or more new bitcoin, because the difficulty adjusts to keep blocks about 10 minutes apart.
example: Say a miner runs machines totalling 10 EH/s on a network of 800 EH/s. Its share is 10 ÷ 800 = 1.25%, so of about 144 blocks a day it can expect 144 × 1.25% = 1.8 blocks. At 3.125 BTC per block, that is 1.8 × 3.125 = 5.625 BTC a day before fees.
formula: Miner's expected share of blocks = Miner's hash rate / Network hash rate

short: A built-in rule that halves the reward of new bitcoins paid to miners roughly every four years, slowing the creation of new coins.
kid: Every few years, the prize for finishing the puzzle gets cut in half. First you got four stickers, then two, then one, so new stickers become rarer and rarer.
detail: A halving is written into Bitcoin's code: every 210,000 blocks, about four years, the block subsidy paid to miners for each new block is cut in half. It began at 50 BTC in 2009 and fell to 25 in 2012, 12.5 in 2016, 6.25 in 2020 and 3.125 in April 2024; the next halving is expected around 2028. Because of this schedule, total supply can never exceed 21 million coins, and more than 90% have already been mined. Halvings hit miners hardest, since their revenue in bitcoin terms drops overnight, so less efficient operators shut down or sell coins. Investors watch them because past halvings came before big price rises, which fuels talk of a four-year cycle. The confusion to avoid: a halving reduces new supply, not the coins people already own, and because it is known years in advance, nothing guarantees it will lift the price.
example: Before the April 2024 halving, about 144 blocks a day × 6.25 BTC = 900 new bitcoin were created daily. Afterwards it was 144 × 3.125 = 450 BTC a day, so a miner earning 10 BTC a day in subsidy dropped to 5 BTC overnight unless its share of the network grew.
formula: Block subsidy = 50 BTC / 2^n, where n = number of halvings so far

short: Using the same digital money twice, for example paying two people with one coin; blockchains exist largely to prevent it.
kid: If you draw a picture of a sweet, you could copy it and give the same sweet to two friends. A careful helper keeps a list so each real sweet can only be given away once.
detail: Digital files are easy to copy, so any digital money must stop the same unit being spent twice. Banks and UPI solve this with a central ledger that debits your account once. Bitcoin's 2008 white paper proposed a way to do it without a trusted middleman: every transaction goes on a public blockchain, and miners include only one of two conflicting payments. A double spend becomes possible if a payee accepts a transaction before it is confirmed, or if an attacker rewrites recent blocks, typically through a 51% attack. That is why exchanges wait for several confirmations, or added blocks, before crediting a deposit, and wait longer on smaller, less secure chains. The confusion to avoid: double spending is not counterfeiting or hacking a wallet; it is getting two conflicting payments of the same coins accepted, usually by reversing one after receiving the goods.
example: Say an exchange credits bitcoin deposits after 6 confirmations. With a new block about every 10 minutes, that is roughly 6 × 10 = 60 minutes. On a smaller coin with 1-minute blocks that is cheaper to attack, the same exchange might demand 120 confirmations, or about 120 × 1 = 120 minutes.

short: An attack in which one group controls more than half of a blockchain's mining power, letting it rewrite recent transactions and spend coins twice.
kid: In a class vote, if one group has more than half the hands, it can change what the class notebook says happened yesterday. It still cannot take toys out of your bag.
detail: In a proof-of-work blockchain, the valid history is the chain with the most accumulated work. An attacker with more than half the network's hash rate can secretly build a longer chain and then release it, replacing recent blocks. That lets it double-spend: pay an exchange, withdraw other coins, then erase the original payment. It can also block other people's transactions. It cannot steal coins from wallets it does not control or break the coin's supply rules. Proof-of-stake chains face the same threat from anyone controlling a large enough share of the staked coins. Bitcoin, with its enormous hash rate, has never suffered one, but smaller coins have: Ethereum Classic was hit several times in 2019 and 2020, and Bitcoin Gold in 2018 and 2020. The confusion to avoid: 51% is not a magic line; an attacker with less can sometimes succeed with luck, and more confirmations make any attack costlier.
example: Say a small coin's honest miners run 40 units of computing power, so an attacker needs more than 40 units to outpace them. If it rents 41 units at $2,000 per unit per hour for 6 hours, the attack costs 41 × 2,000 × 6 = $492,000. It pays only if the coins it can double-spend are worth more than that.
formula: Attacker's share = Attacker's hash rate / (Attacker's hash rate + Honest hash rate); a sustained attack needs this above 50%

short: A change to a blockchain's rules; if some users refuse to upgrade, the chain can split into two separate networks and coins.
kid: Friends are walking down a path playing a game with the same rules. If some want new rules and others do not, the path splits and each group goes its own way.
detail: A blockchain's rules live in software that thousands of independent computers run. A soft fork tightens the rules in a backward-compatible way, so old software still accepts new blocks; Bitcoin's SegWit (2017) and Taproot (2021) upgrades were soft forks. A hard fork changes the rules so that old software rejects new blocks, which means everyone must upgrade. Most hard forks are planned upgrades with broad agreement. When a community disagrees, a hard fork can cause a chain split: Ethereum Classic kept the original chain after Ethereum hard-forked to recover funds lost in the 2016 DAO hack, and Bitcoin Cash split from Bitcoin in August 2017 over block size. Holders at the split own coins on both chains, which raises tax, custody and listing questions. The confusion to avoid: not every fork creates a new coin, and coins from a split are rarely worth as much as the original.
example: Anyone holding 2 BTC when Bitcoin Cash split off on 1 August 2017 also received 2 BCH, because the new chain copied every balance one for one. Say an exchange held 10,000 customer bitcoins at the split: it then also controlled 10,000 BCH and had to decide whether, and when, to credit them to customers.

short: The fee users pay to get a transfer or app action processed on Ethereum and similar blockchains, priced per unit of computing work.
kid: To ride the busy toy train, you give the driver a sticker. When lots of children want a ride at once, the driver asks for more stickers.
detail: On Ethereum, every operation uses a measured amount of computation called gas. A plain ether transfer uses 21,000 gas units; a token swap can use several times more. Users pay for each unit in gwei, one billionth of an ether. Since the London upgrade of August 2021 (EIP-1559), the fee has two parts: a base fee set by the protocol according to demand for block space, which is burned, and an optional priority fee, or tip, paid to the validator. Gas spikes during market frenzies and popular token launches, pricing out small users and pushing activity to cheaper layer 2 networks. Bitcoin also charges network fees, priced by data size. The confusion to avoid: the fee depends on how much computation a transaction needs and how busy the network is, not on how much money is sent, and a failed transaction still pays for the gas it used.
example: Say a simple transfer uses 21,000 gas and the total gas price is 20 gwei. The fee is 21,000 × 20 = 420,000 gwei, or 0.00042 ETH; with ether at an assumed $3,000, that is 0.00042 × 3,000 = $1.26, whether you send $10 or $10 million.
formula: Transaction fee = Gas used × (Base fee + Priority fee)

short: A base blockchain, such as Bitcoin, Ethereum or Solana, that checks and permanently records transactions itself, without relying on another network.
kid: The big main road through town is where every trip finally gets written in the town's record book. Smaller lanes can join it, but the main road keeps the book safe.
detail: A layer 1 (L1) is a blockchain that handles consensus, security and final settlement itself, with its own native coin to pay fees and reward miners or validators. Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche are examples. Each L1 juggles what is often called the blockchain trilemma: being decentralised, secure and fast all at once is hard. Bitcoin handles only about seven transactions per second, by design, so that ordinary computers can verify it; newer L1s process far more but rely on fewer, more powerful machines. Investors treat L1 coins somewhat like shares in a platform, betting that more apps and users will raise demand for block space and the native coin; 'alt L1' describes rivals to Ethereum. The confusion to avoid: L1 does not mean better or older; it describes where transactions are finally settled, and many apps now run on layer 2 networks that settle back onto an L1.
example: Say an L1 adds a block every 12 seconds and each block fits 1,200 transactions. Its throughput is 1,200 ÷ 12 = 100 transactions per second, or 100 × 86,400 = 8.64 million a day. If demand doubles to 200 per second, fees rise until some users wait or leave.
formula: Throughput (transactions per second) = Transactions per block / Block time in seconds

short: A network built on top of a main blockchain that handles transactions faster and more cheaply, then records them on the main chain.
kid: Instead of every child walking to the teacher's desk one by one, a helper collects everyone's notes in one bag. Then the helper takes the whole bag to the teacher in a single trip.
detail: A layer 2 (L2) processes transactions away from its base chain, or layer 1, and regularly posts compressed data or proofs back to it, so users borrow the L1's security while paying lower fees. On Ethereum the main type is the rollup. Optimistic rollups such as Arbitrum, Optimism and Base assume batches are valid unless someone challenges them, which is why standard withdrawals to Ethereum take about seven days. Zero-knowledge rollups such as zkSync and Starknet post cryptographic proofs instead. Bitcoin's Lightning Network uses payment channels for instant small payments. Ethereum's Dencun upgrade in March 2024 created cheaper data space for rollups and cut many L2 fees sharply. The confusion to avoid: a sidechain with its own validators is not a true L2, because its security does not come from the base chain, and many L2s still rely on a single operator to order transactions.
example: Say posting one batch to Ethereum costs $40 and the batch holds 2,000 transfers. Each transfer's share is $40 ÷ 2,000 = $0.02, against perhaps $1.26 for a simple transfer made directly on Ethereum at the same moment, about 63 times more.
formula: L1 data cost per L2 transaction = Cost of posting a batch to L1 / Transactions in the batch

short: Turning ownership of a real asset, such as a bond, fund unit, building or gold, into digital tokens on a blockchain.
kid: A big cake is cut into lots of small slices, and each slice gets a name card. Whoever holds a card owns that slice and can swap the card with a friend.
detail: Tokenisation issues a digital token on a blockchain that represents a legal claim on an asset held off-chain, such as Treasury bills, money market fund units, private credit, property or gold. Tokens can be split into small fractions, transferred around the clock and settled in minutes, and smart contracts can automate payouts and compliance checks. The biggest use so far is tokenised US Treasuries and money market funds, such as BlackRock's BUIDL fund launched in 2024, which crypto firms use as collateral that earns interest. Banks also test tokenised deposits. In India, fractional ownership of property is offered through SEBI-regulated REITs and small and medium REITs, which do not use blockchains. The confusion to avoid: a token is only as good as the legal structure and custodian behind it, and asset tokenisation is different from card tokenisation, the RBI-mandated replacement of card numbers with tokens for online payments.
example: Say a ₹50 crore office building is tokenised into 5 lakh tokens, so each token represents ₹50 crore ÷ 5,00,000 = ₹1,000 of the property. An investor who buys 250 tokens for ₹2,50,000 owns 0.05% of it; if net annual rent is ₹4 crore, their share is ₹4 crore × 0.05% = ₹20,000.
formula: Value per token = Value of the underlying asset / Number of tokens issued

short: The combined value of all cryptocurrencies, found by multiplying each coin's price by the number of coins in circulation and adding them up.
kid: Count how many marbles every child in the playground has, and what each kind of marble is worth. Add it all up and you know how big the whole marble game is.
detail: Crypto market capitalisation applies the stock-market idea of market cap to digital assets. For one coin it is price times circulating supply; the total crypto market cap adds this up across thousands of coins, including stablecoins, as tracked by data sites such as CoinGecko, whose figures differ slightly. It is the headline gauge of the sector's size and mood: the total reached about $3 trillion in November 2021, then fell below $1 trillion during the 2022 crypto winter. A small coin with a tiny tradable supply can show a huge market cap that could never be realised in a sale, and fully diluted valuation, which counts tokens not yet released, can be far higher. The confusion to avoid: market cap is not the money invested; the last trade sets the price for every coin, so a modest inflow can add a large amount of market cap.
example: Say a token has 100 million coins circulating out of a maximum of 1 billion, and trades at $2. Its market cap is 100 million × $2 = $200 million, but its fully diluted valuation is 1 billion × $2 = $2 billion, ten times higher, because 900 million coins are still to be released.
formula: Crypto market capitalisation = Sum of (Price × Circulating supply) across all crypto assets

short: Bitcoin's share of the total value of all cryptocurrencies, used to gauge whether money is flowing into bitcoin or into other coins.
kid: If there are ten slices of pie on the table and the biggest eater has six, that friend has six out of every ten. This tells you how much of the pie belongs to the biggest one.
detail: Bitcoin dominance divides bitcoin's market capitalisation by the total crypto market cap; charting sites list it under the ticker BTC.D. Bitcoin had almost the whole market in its early years. Dominance fell below 40% in early 2018 during the initial coin offering boom, when money poured into new tokens, and climbed back above 60% in 2025 as spot bitcoin ETFs drew institutional money. Traders read a rising figure as investors favouring the larger, more liquid coin, and a falling one as the start of an 'altcoin season', when smaller coins outperform. The confusion to avoid: dominance is a ratio, so it can rise while bitcoin's price falls, if other coins fall faster; and because stablecoins count in the total, growth in stablecoin supply lowers bitcoin's share even when nobody is buying other coins.
example: Say bitcoin's market cap is $1.2 trillion and the whole crypto market is $2 trillion: dominance is 1.2 ÷ 2 = 60%. If other coins then lose a quarter of their $0.8 trillion while bitcoin stays flat, the total becomes $1.8 trillion and dominance rises to 1.2 ÷ 1.8 = 66.7%.
formula: Bitcoin dominance = Bitcoin market capitalisation / Total crypto market capitalisation × 100

short: An exchange-traded fund that holds actual bitcoin, letting investors bet on bitcoin's price by buying fund units through an ordinary broker.
kid: Instead of keeping a special coin in your own box, a trusted grown-up locks lots of coins in a safe. You get a ticket for your part of the pile, and you can swap the ticket easily.
detail: A spot bitcoin ETF buys and holds real bitcoin through a regulated custodian and issues shares that trade on a stock exchange, so the share price tracks bitcoin minus a yearly fee. The US Securities and Exchange Commission approved the first 11 on 10 January 2024; spot ether ETFs followed in July 2024, and funds on other tokens in late 2025. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust became one of the fastest-growing ETFs ever, and daily ETF inflows and outflows are now a closely watched driver of bitcoin's price. Indian residents cannot buy these on Indian exchanges; they can invest via overseas brokers under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme, within its limits as of 2025. The confusion to avoid: a spot ETF holds the coin itself, while a bitcoin futures ETF holds futures contracts and can lag the price because of rolling costs; and ETF investors cannot withdraw coins to their own wallet.
example: Say a spot bitcoin ETF holds 5,000 BTC and bitcoin is at an assumed $80,000, so its assets are 5,000 × $80,000 = $400 million. With 10 million shares outstanding, each share's NAV is $40, and at a 0.25% annual expense ratio the fund charges $400 million × 0.25% = $1 million a year.
formula: NAV per share = (Bitcoin held × Bitcoin price − Liabilities) / Shares outstanding

short: A listed company whose main strategy is raising money to buy and hold bitcoin or other crypto, making the coins its main asset.
kid: A shop stops caring much about selling lemonade and uses its money to collect shiny marbles instead. People buy a piece of the shop because they want a piece of the marble pile.
detail: A digital asset treasury company (DAT) sells shares, convertible bonds or preferred stock and uses the money to accumulate crypto. MicroStrategy, now Strategy, pioneered the model when it began buying bitcoin in August 2020; in 2025 dozens of companies copied it with bitcoin, ether, Solana and other tokens. The key number is mNAV, the company's market value divided by the value of its crypto. When mNAV is above 1, issuing new shares to buy more coins raises the crypto held per share, feeding a self-reinforcing loop. When it falls below 1, the loop stops working, and some DATs have bought back shares or sold coins instead; many saw their premiums collapse in late 2025 as crypto prices fell. The confusion to avoid: buying a DAT is not the same as owning the coins, because you also take on operating costs, debt, dilution and swings in the premium.
example: Say XYZ Corp has 100 million shares at $12, a market value of $1.2 billion, and holds 10,000 BTC worth $800 million at an assumed $80,000 each, so its mNAV is 1.2 ÷ 0.8 = 1.5. It sells 10 million new shares at $12 for $120 million and buys 1,500 BTC. Bitcoin per share rises from 10,000 ÷ 100 million = 0.0001 to 11,500 ÷ 110 million, about 0.0001045, roughly 4.5% higher.
formula: mNAV = Market capitalisation / Market value of crypto holdings

short: Safekeeping of the secret keys that control crypto assets, done either by the owner or by a specialist firm on investors' behalf.
kid: Your special coin only opens with a secret password. You can hide the password yourself, or give it to a trusted helper who locks it in a strong safe.
detail: Whoever holds the private key to a crypto address can move the coins, so custody means protecting keys, not storing a physical asset. Investors can self-custody in their own wallets, or use custodians such as Coinbase, BitGo, Anchorage or, increasingly, traditional banks. Institutional custodians keep most assets in cold storage, offline and split across several keys and locations, with a small share in online hot wallets for withdrawals, and should keep client assets segregated from their own. Failures are costly: FTX's 2022 collapse showed customer coins being misused, and India's WazirX lost about $230 million of user assets in a July 2024 hack. Indian crypto platforms must register with FIU-IND for anti-money-laundering purposes, but no specific custody rules exist as of 2025. The confusion to avoid: if an exchange fails, coins left on it may turn out to be only an unsecured claim against it.
example: Say a custodian looks after $50 million of bitcoin for a fund and charges 0.20% a year, a fee of $50 million × 0.20% = $100,000. It keeps 95%, or $47.5 million, offline in cold storage and only $2.5 million in hot wallets, which caps what a single online hack could steal at 5% of the total.

short: A check, often by an outside firm, showing that a crypto exchange holds enough coins to cover what it owes all its customers.
kid: A toy library says it is keeping everyone's toys safe. Proof of reserves is when it opens the cupboard and counts, so everyone can see their toys are really there.
detail: Proof of reserves (PoR) became common after FTX collapsed in November 2022 with a large hole between customer balances and actual assets. A typical PoR has two halves. On the asset side, the exchange proves it controls specific blockchain addresses, for example by signing a message with their keys, so anyone can check the balances. On the liability side, it takes a snapshot of all customer balances, arranges them in a Merkle tree, a cryptographic summary, and lets each customer confirm their balance was included. A reserve ratio of 100% or more suggests coins are fully backed. The limits are serious: it is a snapshot, so coins can be borrowed for the day; it may leave out loans and other debts; and it is not a full audit. The confusion to avoid: proof of reserves shows that assets exist, not that the exchange is solvent.
example: Say an exchange's customers are owed 12,000 BTC in total and its signed addresses show 12,600 BTC. Its reserve ratio is 12,600 ÷ 12,000 = 105%. If 1,000 of those coins were borrowed just before the snapshot, true reserves are 11,600 BTC, a ratio of about 96.7%.
formula: Reserve ratio = Verified customer assets held / Total customer liabilities × 100

short: A never-expiring futures contract for betting on crypto prices, kept close to the market price by regular payments between buyers and sellers.
kid: Two friends make a bet about whether a toy will get costlier, and the bet never has to end. Every few hours, one hands the other a sweet so the bet stays fair.
detail: Perpetual futures, or perps, were introduced by BitMEX in 2016 and are now the most traded crypto product, with volumes typically several times those of spot markets. Like ordinary futures, they let traders go long or short on margin, often at 10x leverage or more on offshore venues. Unlike ordinary futures, they never expire, so there is no rollover and no convergence to spot on a settlement date. Instead, a funding rate, exchanged between longs and shorts every few hours, pulls the perp price back towards the spot index. Positions are closed automatically when margin runs low. Perps trade on centralised exchanges and on decentralised ones such as Hyperliquid; as of 2025, some FIU-registered Indian platforms also offer them, outside SEBI's F&O framework. The confusion to avoid: a perp is not the coin itself, and holding one for months can cost a lot in funding.
example: Say you go long 1 BTC on a perp at an assumed $80,000, posting $8,000 of margin (10x leverage). If the price falls 5% to $76,000, you lose $4,000, half your margin. If funding is +0.01% every 8 hours, you also pay $80,000 × 0.01% = $8 per period, or $24 a day, to the shorts.
formula: Profit on a long perpetual = (Exit price − Entry price) × Position size − Net funding paid

short: A small, regular payment between buyers and sellers of perpetual futures that keeps the contract price close to the coin's actual market price.
kid: If too many children crowd onto one end of a seesaw, they each give a sweet to the children on the other end. That makes some switch sides until it balances.
detail: On perpetual futures, the exchange calculates a funding rate every few hours, commonly every eight. When the perp trades above the spot price, the rate is positive and traders holding longs pay those holding shorts; when it trades below, the rate turns negative and shorts pay longs. The payment passes between traders, not to the exchange, and only those holding a position at the funding time pay or receive it. On many exchanges the formula settles at 0.01% per eight hours when markets are calm. Traders watch funding as a sentiment gauge: very high positive rates signal crowded, leveraged bullish bets that can unwind in a liquidation cascade. Funds also earn it through a basis trade, buying the coin and shorting the perp. The confusion to avoid: a rate that looks tiny per period adds up, as 0.01% every eight hours is about 11% a year.
example: Say you hold a $50,000 long perp and funding is +0.03% per eight hours. You pay $50,000 × 0.03% = $15 each period, or $45 a day; annualised, 0.03% × 3 × 365 = 32.85%, a heavy cost for holding the bet for long.
formula: Funding payment = Position notional value × Funding rate

short: A crypto scam in which a project's creators suddenly take investors' money or dump their own tokens, leaving the token almost worthless.
kid: Someone builds a lemonade stand and lots of friends give coins to share in it. Then the builder grabs the coin jar and runs away.
detail: In a rug pull, developers promote a new token or project, attract buyers, then vanish with the money, pulling the rug from under investors. Common methods are withdrawing the coins that back a token's trading pool on a decentralised exchange, selling a large hidden stash of tokens, or using code that stops buyers from selling, sometimes called a honeypot. The Squid Game token, named after the Netflix show, crashed to almost zero in November 2021 after its developers cashed out; buyers had been unable to sell. Warning signs include anonymous founders, unaudited code, trading-pool funds that are not locked, a few wallets holding most of the supply, and promises of guaranteed returns. The confusion to avoid: a rug pull is deliberate fraud by insiders, unlike a hack by outsiders or a crash in a genuine project. In India, victims can file cybercrime complaints, but recovery is rare.
example: Say a new token's trading pool holds $500,000 of ether and its anonymous developers secretly hold 40% of the supply. They sell their tokens into the pool and withdraw the ether, and the price drops 99%. An investor who put in $2,000 is left with $2,000 × 1% = $20.

short: Crypto slang for holding an asset for the long run instead of selling during price swings, born from a misspelling of 'hold'.
kid: You get a shiny marble and keep it safe for a long, long time. Even when friends say it looks dull today, you hold on to it.
detail: HODL began on 18 December 2013, when a user on the Bitcointalk forum, frustrated during a price crash, posted a rambling message titled 'I AM HODLING'. The typo became a rallying cry, later explained as 'hold on for dear life'. A hodler buys and holds through booms and crashes, betting on long-term adoption rather than trading, and analysts track the supply held by 'long-term holders', coins unmoved for about 155 days or more, as a sentiment measure. It is crypto's version of buy and hold, and it rewarded early bitcoin buyers who sat through repeated falls of 70% or more. The confusion to avoid: HODL is a mindset, not risk management. Holding works only if the asset recovers, many tokens never do, and investors should size crypto so that a deep drawdown does not force them to sell at the bottom.
example: Bitcoin peaked near $69,000 in November 2021 and fell to about $15,500 a year later, a drop of (69,000 − 15,500) ÷ 69,000, about 77.5%. A hodler needed a gain of about 345% from that low just to break even, which bitcoin achieved in March 2024 when it passed its old high.

short: A long stretch, often a year or more, of falling crypto prices, low trading activity, layoffs and scarce funding across the crypto industry.
kid: In winter the lemonade stand gets very few customers for a long time. Some stands close, and the ones that stay open wait patiently for spring.
detail: A crypto winter is the sector's version of a prolonged bear market. The first widely named one followed the 2017 boom: bitcoin fell about 84% between December 2017 and December 2018, and many tokens from initial coin offerings went to zero. The 2022 winter did more damage: the TerraUSD stablecoin and its sister token Luna collapsed in May, lenders Celsius and Voyager and the fund Three Arrows Capital failed, and FTX went bankrupt in November. Winters bring falling prices and volumes, exchange layoffs and a slump in venture funding. In India, 2022 also brought the 30% tax and 1% TDS, after which volumes on Indian exchanges fell sharply and many traders moved to offshore platforms. The confusion to avoid: a crash lasting a few days is not a winter; the term means a long period, and calling the bottom in real time is very hard.
example: Bitcoin fell from nearly $20,000 in December 2017 to about $3,200 in December 2018, a drop of (20,000 − 3,200) ÷ 20,000 = 84%. A ₹1 lakh holding that fell 84% would be worth ₹16,000, and would need to rise 525% to get back to ₹1 lakh.

short: India's crypto tax rules: a flat 30% on gains, no offsetting of losses, and 1% deducted on most sales, under the rules as of 2025.
kid: When you win sweets by swapping special cards, the grown-ups take a big bite of what you won. If you lose sweets on another swap, that does not make the bite any smaller.
detail: From 1 April 2022, Section 115BBH of the Income-tax Act 1961 taxes income from transferring virtual digital assets (VDAs), including crypto and NFTs, at a flat 30%, under the rules as of 2025, plus surcharge and 4% cess, whatever the holding period or the person's slab. Only the cost of acquisition can be deducted. Losses cannot be set off against any other income, not even gains on another VDA, and cannot be carried forward. From 1 July 2022, Section 194S added 1% TDS on the sale value of VDA transfers above small annual thresholds, creating a trail visible in Form 26AS. The regime carried into the Income-tax Act 2025, in force from April 2026, under new section numbers. The confusion to avoid: rates can change in any Budget; and the TDS is not an extra tax but a credit against your final bill.
example: Say you buy a token for ₹2,00,000 and sell it on an Indian exchange for ₹2,60,000, so the exchange deducts 1% TDS of ₹2,600. Tax on the ₹60,000 gain is 30%, or ₹18,000, plus 4% cess of ₹720, ₹18,720 in all, ignoring surcharge. After the TDS credit you owe ₹16,120 more, and a ₹25,000 loss on another token that year cannot reduce it.
formula: Tax on VDA gains = 30% × (Sale value − Cost of acquisition), plus surcharge and 4% cess; TDS = 1% × Sale value
related: Set-off and carry forward of losses

short: The European Union's single rulebook for crypto, licensing crypto exchanges and issuers of price-stable coins so one approval covers all 27 member countries.
kid: Lots of neighbouring towns agreed on one set of rules for a new kind of sticker shop. A shop that gets permission in one town may open in all of them.
detail: MiCA, Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, is the first comprehensive crypto law across a major economic bloc. Its stablecoin rules apply from 30 June 2024 and the rest from 30 December 2024. Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs), such as exchanges, brokers and custodians, need authorisation from one national regulator and can then passport across the EU, with rules on capital, custody of client assets, conflicts of interest and complaints. Stablecoin issuers must hold reserves, offer redemption on demand and meet stricter limits once they become significant; MiCA separates e-money tokens, tied to one official currency, from asset-referenced tokens. It also adds market-abuse rules and white-paper disclosures. Afterwards, several exchanges restricted non-compliant stablecoins, notably Tether's USDT, for EU users. The confusion to avoid: MiCA does not cover crypto that already counts as a financial instrument under EU securities law, or fully decentralised DeFi. India has no comparable crypto law as of 2025.
example: Before MiCA, an exchange serving all 27 EU countries could need separate national registrations in many of them; under MiCA, one licence from a single national regulator covers all 27. Firms already operating under national rules could continue for up to about 18 months after 30 December 2024, until 1 July 2026 at the latest.

aliases: Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins Act
hl: guiding and establishing national innovation for us stablecoins act
guiding and establishing national innovation for u.s. stablecoins act
short: The 2025 US law regulating stablecoins, crypto tokens tied to the dollar, by requiring licensed issuers and full backing with cash-like assets.
kid: If you give a shopkeeper one coin for a paper ticket, the shopkeeper must keep your coin safe in a box. New rules make sure every ticket really has a coin behind it.
detail: The Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for US Stablecoins (GENIUS) Act became law on 18 July 2025, the first major US federal crypto statute. Only permitted issuers, such as bank subsidiaries and approved non-bank firms, may issue payment stablecoins to US users; issuers with up to $10 billion outstanding can opt for state supervision. Every coin must be backed at least 1:1 by cash, bank deposits, Treasury bills maturing within 93 days, certain repos or government money market funds, with monthly public reserve reports. Issuers must follow anti-money-laundering rules, cannot pay interest to holders, and holders get priority if an issuer fails. It matters because issuers are big buyers of Treasury bills. Most rules take effect once regulators write them, by January 2027 at the latest. The confusion to avoid: GENIUS covers only stablecoins; wider crypto market rules sit in the separate CLARITY Act.
example: Say a hypothetical issuer, ABC Dollar, has $20 billion of stablecoins outstanding. It must hold at least $20 billion of eligible reserves and, being above the $10 billion threshold, must generally move under federal supervision. If those reserves earn an assumed 4% a year, it collects $20 billion × 4% = $800 million but cannot pay any of it to holders as interest.

short: A US government stockpile of bitcoin, created in 2025 from coins seized in legal cases, which the government says it will hold rather than sell.
kid: A grown-up keeps the special coins that were taken from people who broke the rules. Instead of selling them, the grown-up puts them in a big jar and saves them.
detail: On 6 March 2025, a US executive order created the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, funded with bitcoin the federal government already owned through criminal and civil forfeitures, such as coins seized in the Silk Road case. The order says these coins should not be sold and treats them as a long-term reserve asset; a separate Digital Asset Stockpile holds other forfeited tokens. Further purchases were allowed only through budget-neutral means, so no taxpayer money was committed. Several US states, including Texas and New Hampshire, passed their own reserve laws in 2025, while El Salvador and Bhutan already held bitcoin. Supporters compare bitcoin to gold; critics point to its volatility and lack of income. The confusion to avoid: the reserve did not begin with large new purchases, and India's foreign exchange reserves, managed by the RBI, hold foreign currencies, gold, SDRs and an IMF reserve position, not crypto.
example: Say a hypothetical country holds 10,000 seized BTC within total reserves of $100 billion. At an assumed $80,000 per bitcoin, the coins are worth 10,000 × $80,000 = $800 million, or 0.8% of reserves. If bitcoin's price halves, total reserves fall by $400 million, just 0.4%, which is why a small allocation is easier to defend than a large one.

short: The Indian legal term for cryptocurrencies, NFTs and similar digital tokens, used mainly in tax and anti-money-laundering rules.
kid: Grown-ups needed one name for all kinds of computer coins and computer trading cards. So they put them all in one box with one label.
detail: Section 2(47A) of the Income-tax Act 1961, added in 2022, defines a virtual digital asset (VDA) as any information, code, number or token, other than Indian or foreign currency, generated through cryptographic or similar means and providing a digital representation of value. It covers bitcoin, stablecoins and NFTs. The government excluded gift cards, vouchers, reward and mileage points and website subscriptions, and the RBI's digital rupee is currency, not a VDA. The label triggers the 30% tax and 1% TDS regime, under the rules as of 2025, which carried into the Income-tax Act 2025. Since March 2023, VDA service providers, including offshore exchanges serving Indians, must register with FIU-IND. The confusion to avoid: being a VDA does not make something legal tender or SEBI-regulated; crypto in India is neither banned nor fully regulated, after the Supreme Court in 2020 struck down the RBI's 2018 curbs on banks serving crypto firms.
example: Say Meera holds an NFT bought for ₹10,000, ₹5,000 of bitcoin and 2,000 airline miles. The NFT and the bitcoin are VDAs; the miles are excluded. If she sells the NFT for ₹16,000, the ₹6,000 gain is taxed at 30%, or ₹1,800 before cess and surcharge.

short: A US bill that would split oversight of crypto markets between the securities and commodities regulators and set rules for crypto exchanges and brokers.
kid: Two playground teachers kept arguing about who should watch a new game. This plan says which teacher watches which part, so the players know the rules.
detail: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, H.R. 3633, aims to end years of 'regulation by enforcement' by stating which US regulator oversees which crypto activity. Under the House version, tokens whose value depends on a mature, decentralised blockchain are digital commodities whose spot trading is supervised by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), while fundraising by token issuers stays under Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) disclosure rules. Exchanges, brokers and dealers would register, segregate customer assets and meet disclosure standards. The House passed it with bipartisan support in July 2025, alongside the GENIUS Act; the Senate then worked on its own drafts, with disputes over issues such as exchanges paying rewards on stablecoins, and it had not become law as of early 2026, so check its latest status. The confusion to avoid: CLARITY is about who regulates crypto trading, while GENIUS covers only stablecoins.
example: Say a US exchange lists 200 tokens. If 180 qualify as digital commodities and 20 as investment contract assets still under SEC rules, then under the House version 180 ÷ 200 = 90% of its listings would fall under CFTC oversight and 10% under the SEC.

short: A chain reaction in which falling prices force the automatic closing of borrowed-money bets, whose selling pushes prices lower and triggers more closures.
kid: A long row of dominoes stands close together. When the first one falls it knocks over the next, and soon the whole row tumbles down.
detail: Crypto traders often use high leverage on perpetual futures. When the price moves against a position and its margin falls below the maintenance level, the exchange's engine closes it automatically with a market order. In a falling market those forced sales push the price down further, which hits the liquidation prices of the next layer of leveraged longs, and so on: a long squeeze. The same can happen upwards, forcing shorts to buy. Thin order books, round-the-clock trading and leverage of 20x or more make cascades fast and violent; on 10-11 October 2025, more than $19 billion of positions were liquidated in about a day, the largest such wipeout on record. Traders watch open interest, funding rates and maps of where liquidation prices cluster. The confusion to avoid: this 'liquidation' means the forced closing of a trading position, not a company being wound up.
example: Say you go long 1.25 BTC at an assumed $80,000, a $100,000 position backed by $10,000 of margin (10x). A 10% fall to $72,000 loses 1.25 × $8,000 = $10,000, wiping out the margin, so the exchange liquidates you slightly before that. If thousands of such positions sit near $72,000, their forced selling can drive the price on to the next cluster of liquidation prices.
formula: Approximate liquidation price of a long = Entry price × (1 − 1 / Leverage), ignoring maintenance margin and fees
